cover.title: One [[dt|test harness]]
cover.lead: One command runs every test suite from one list and reports in one result format, and a run that tested nothing can never come out green.
cover.notes: Source: docs/internals/rfcs/rfc-29-test-harness.md, commit 06b1e48. The RFC describes the harness the project wants to end up with; this deck follows its fifth revision. Keys: → next, S speaker notes. Click any underlined term for its definition.

intro.two: One Go command, [[dt]], runs every test [[suite]] the same way on a laptop and in CI: it reads one [[registry|list of suites]], builds the DittoFS server each one needs, calls the test tool and [[grade|grades]] every result against lists of [[known-failure|known failures]]. It exists because a green result did not always mean something was tested, failures on develop went unnoticed, and most tests could not block a merge.
intro.twoNotes: From the Summary ('The problem', 'The proposal') and 'Start here · In plain words'.
intro.knownLead: RFC 29 builds on no other RFC, because it is about the test tooling rather than the server. The DittoFS terms below appear in it only in passing. Click one to read its definition.
intro.knownNotes: The RFC index says RFC 29 builds on no other RFC, RFC 0 included. Share: a fixture's shares (§4.2). Adapter: the NFS and SMB adapters a fixture enables (§4.2). Lease: the fixture's NFSv4 lease (§4.2). The journal, syncer and engine appear only as example component groups (§4.9).
intro.newNotes: RFC 29 has no glossary section; each term is defined where the RFC introduces it: dt (§3), registry, suite, option, group (§4.1), cell (§4.4), store profile and fixture (§4.2), needs, dtc and the dedicated host (§4.4, §4.5), the system scenarios (§1, §4.1), tier and blocking (§4.3), gate (§4.8), format, CTRF, grade (§4.6), known failure, expected skip, unexpected pass, quarantine, flaky, retry (§4.7), not run (§4.4, R10), the develop-red issue (§4.8). The glossary at the end adds matrix, shard and client lease.
intro.clashNotes: Tier: DittoFS's storage tiers (RFC 0, RFC 4) versus RFC 29's test tiers (§4.3). Fixture: the usual test-code sense versus §4.2's whole server. Gate: the gate job (§4.8) versus the performance and allocation gates (§4.10) and the adapters' share gate. Store profile versus performance and coverage profiles (§4.1's unit suite writes a coverage profile). Lease: the fixture's NFSv4 lease (§4.2).

ways.title: Before [[dt]] (October 2026), every [[suite]] ran its own way
ways.w1: test suites, and each one was started and reported its results in its own way
ways.w2: CI workflows, which started about 30 jobs for every pull request that changed more than documentation
ways.w3: glue scripts, about 8,900 lines in all, sat between CI and the test tools
ways.w4: places where the same server setup was written out again
ways.w5: was how long a pull request waited for its slowest workflow to finish
ways.w6: kinds of check could block a merge: unit tests, integration tests, lint and security scans
ways.notes: Summary and §1 Why. The script count: 35 of the 92 shell scripts under test/ and .github/scripts/; the Summary says about 8,900 lines, §3 and Appendix A about 8,860. Server setup written in at least five places: the two bootstrap.sh, setup-posix.sh and two jobs of smb-client-compat.yml. PR times: 2026-10-07, 300 PR workflow runs; Conformance Suites 23 min median and 39 at p90. Required checks: lint and security only until 2026-10-08, then Unit and Integration Tests too. These figures are the RFC's own measurements from October 2026, taken before dt: they show the problem the RFC answers, not the state of CI after it.

silent.title: Green that tested nothing
table: pjdfstest and pynfs runs that store data in S3 (`badger-s3`)
Nothing created their S3 bucket, so every request got `NoSuchBucket` back. The NFSv4 pjdfstest run still graded 8,789 tests green.
The client could not load the NFS module in its container, so it printed “skipping test” and exited 0, which counts as a pass.
11 subtests were skipped on every run, while the tests that contain them reported a pass.
WPTS is Microsoft's test suite for SMB, and BVT is its basic set. 70 of those 335 tests never ran, and they were counted as skips with no list of which skips are expected.
The Go integration test of portmap
Its result did not come from a new run. It was replayed from Go's test cache.
silent.footer: On 2026-10-08, a check of every test workflow's latest green runs found 14 such cases, and each was filed as an issue. In every one, a setup problem, a missing tool or a skipped test was read as a pass.
silent.notes: §1, the table 'Green results that test nothing' (abridged), and the Summary. Others in the table: pynfs runs only its `all` flag (601 of 689 in 4.0, 184 of 266 in 4.1), the smb-client-compat Windows job, the performance gates skipping under -race and -short. WPTS is Microsoft's Windows Protocol Test Suites; its wpts entry runs the tests with TestCategory=BVT (§4.1). The portmap test is an option of the integration suite, built with the portmap_system tag (§4.1); §1 calls it the portmap system test.

unheard.title: Red that nobody heard
items: The nightly conformance run had failed every night since 2026-09-10, while the job that summarised it stayed green.
The AD-DC suite, which tests DittoFS against an Active Directory domain controller, failed on every run on develop after one pull request broke it, and nobody was told.
The alarm that warned when develop went red, an e-mail and an issue, was removed, because [[flaky]] smbtorture subtests set it off all the time.

In October 2026, the 42 [[system-scenario|system scenarios]], scripts that run a real server and real clients and often inject a fault, ran twice a day on a dedicated host, outside every CI job. About half failed on purpose, because they reproduce open bugs, but no list said which ones.
unheard.notes: §1, 'Nobody hears when develop goes red' and 'Scenarios carry no signal'. The nightly failure: its baseline job pushes to develop and the ruleset refuses (#2997). AD-DC: one test still asked for the removed memory metadata store. The alarm (e-mail and issue) was added in #1170 and removed in #1705 (Appendix A). The system scenarios: §4.1's system entry ('a real server in a container, real clients, faults injected'). AD-DC: an option of the integration suite, run against the AD-DC service container (§4.1, §3). The slide describes October 2026, before dt. A gate that needs every blocking job is what stops a failing job from hiding behind a green summary, as the nightly's baseline job did (§4.8).

wrappers.title: Wrappers around wrappers
wrappers.notes: §1 'Wrappers around wrappers' and 'The same work written several times'; §3 ('dt is the one entry point, and it calls each tool itself'); §6, the rejected alternative 'Keeping each suite's scripts and wrapping them'. The scene shows pjdfstest; conformance.yml and tests.yml are the workflows before and after (§4.8, §8).

card.title: One report card for every subject
card.analogy: Each teacher grades differently, but the card uses one scale. On this card “absent” is never written as “passed”: a [[suite]] that didn't run says so.
card.stops: A report card forgets last term. [[dt]] remembers past runs, so “is this test [[flaky]]?” has an answer.
card.footer: In this analogy the teachers are the test tools, and the shared scale is one [[result-format|result format]] with one set of [[grade|grades]].
card.notes: The analogy and where it stops are the RFC's own: 'Start here · In plain words'. The last line is this deck's mapping of the analogy onto §4.6 (formats, grades).

flow.title: What one run does
steps: `dt plan` reads the list of suites in `test/suites.yaml` and expands each [[suite]] into [[cell|cells]], one for each combination of settings it must run with.
For each cell, `dt` starts the DittoFS server the cell needs, called its [[fixture]], and checks that it works before any test runs.
It calls the test tool directly: `go test`, `prove`, `pynfs`, `smbtorture`, WPTS, `fio`.
It reads the tool's own results and [[grade|grades]] them against the [[known-failure|known failures]], [[expected-skip|expected skips]] and [[quarantine]].
It writes one set of results, as [[ctrf|CTRF]] and JUnit files and a report, and the terminal, CI, the GitHub issues and `dt history` all read that same set.
flow.footer: The tools are the ones the suites already use. The registry, the planner, the fixtures, the grading and the result files are new.
flow.notes: §4, the flowchart at the top of Design and the paragraph under it.

decision.title: A command-line tool, written in Go
decision.cli: A service that runs tests needs a host, authentication and a deployment, and a laptop would talk to it differently from CI. Other programs build on files instead: the [[registry]], the lists of known failures, the `summary.json` results and the exit code.
decision.go: An earlier `dt`, written in bash, was one 1,270-line script. What the RFC adds is data handling — YAML, results, grading — which in bash needs `yq` and `jq` and can't reasonably be tested. In Go it has tests and runs on Linux, macOS and Windows.
decision.footer: That bash version is not carried forward. It stays only as the reference for the commands people already use.
decision.notes: §3 Decision: 'A CLI, not an API service' and 'In Go, from the start'. Go's dependencies are already in go.mod (gopkg.in/yaml.v3, cobra). Rejected alternatives in §6: an API service, bash first then Go. The other rejected alternatives (§6): a descriptor file per test, a suite per variant (the second draft's 30 suites), a result kind per tool, selecting suites by changed layer, keeping suites.json, keeping each suite's scripts and wrapping them, make or a Taskfile (named commands but no matrix, needs, fixtures or grading), commands as shell strings, Markdown known-failure lists, JUnit or a schema of our own, retrying on pull requests, an issue per failing test per run, a self-hosted runner on the dedicated host, a merge queue now.

carries.title: What moves into `dt`, and what goes
items: The commands people use today stay as aliases, so `dt unit` means `dt run unit`.
The rules of today's graders move into Go, and their test cases become test data for `dt`.
Facts that only the scripts knew move too, each with a test. For example, pjdfstest needs NFSv4 delegations turned off, and NFSv4.0 callbacks need a server address that is not loopback.
The [[known-failure|known-failure]] lists carry over as data, and so do `dfsbench`, DittoFS's benchmark tool, and `setup.sh`, the script that runs the [[system-scenario|system scenarios]].
carries.goes: 35 of the 92 shell scripts under `test/` and `.github/scripts/` are deleted, about 8,860 lines. They are the dispatcher, each suite's setup, run and grading scripts, the runners around `go test`, the NFS `sec=krb5` conformance job, and the Makefile's `test-*` targets.
carries.footer: Shell stays only where it fits by nature. That means the [[dtc|dtc container]], a Linux container with the pinned test tools in which `dt` can run, the containers that start test services, and the host that runs the system scenarios. No suite gets a new script between `dt` and its test tool.
carries.notes: §3, 'What carries over', 'What goes' and 'What stays'. The full list of what the scripts know includes pynfs's 4.1 tree testing NFSv4.2 unless --minorversion is given, the 10-second settings watcher, pjdfstest's mount options and the Kerberos upcall details. nfstest's knfsd baseline stays, as a dispatch-only evidence job (§3). dtc: §4.4 (--in host|container|auto) and §4.5's places table ('pinned Linux toolchain, privileged'). What goes also lists the runners around go test (run-e2e.sh and the run.sh of ad-dc, kerberos and portmap) and the NFS sec=krb5 conformance job, whose mounts the e2e suite's Kerberos tests cover (§3).

registry.title: One file lists every [[suite]]
items: Each suite finds its own tests, through `go test`, a file glob or pynfs, so adding a test changes no shared file.
Adding a suite takes one line, like the `nfs-mount-smoke` entry.
A variant of a suite is an [[suite-option|option]] of it, not a separate suite, for example `integration --kerberos` or `unit --windows`.
A [[suite-group|group]] gives a set of suites one name, so `dt run conformance` runs every suite in that group.
registry.notes: §4.1 The registry, abridged from its YAML (nfs-mount-smoke is the RFC's hypothetical one-line suite). R2, R3. dt refuses a file that doesn't match the format: unknown fields, a newer version, a missing known file, an unknown placeholder (exit 3).

cells.title: From a [[suite]] to [[cell|cells]]
table: The cells `dt plan` makes from it
items: `dt plan` makes one cell for each combination of the matrix values. Each cell has its own results and exit status, and its own [[fixture]] when the suite has one. In CI each cell runs as a job of its own, except those the [[dedicated-host|dedicated host]] runs itself.
A cell's name joins, with slashes, the suite, its [[suite-option|option]], its matrix values and last its [[test-shard|shard]], as in `smbtorture/badger-s3/shard-2`.
`dt run` also accepts the start of a name, so `dt run pjdfstest/badger-s3` runs all three cells above.
cells.notes: §4.1 (matrix field), §4.4 'Cells'. The prefix rule: 'dt run … runs every cell whose name begins with those segments' (§4.4); the pjdfstest example is this deck's application of it. CI turns dt plan --json into its matrix (§4.8). A fixture is optional: the system suite has none (§4.2). CI's plan keeps every cell but the dedicated host's, which that host runs itself (§4.5, §4.8).

fixture.title: A [[fixture]]: the server the tests run against
items: A fixture is a `dfs` server built from the checkout and started on a [[store-profile|store profile]]: `memory`, `badger` or `badger-s3`.
When the suite needs a mount, the fixture also mounts the share over NFS or SMB. Otherwise it only exports it.
The fixture's [[share|shares]] and users come from data files and from fields of the suite's entry.
Its settings are fields too: squashing, delegations, Kerberos, a reset of the share before each test, and the NFSv4 [[client-lease|client lease]].
fixture.noScript: There is no field for a setup script. A need the fields can't express becomes a new field in `dt`, with a test, so the setup stays in one place.
fixture.notes: §4.2 Fixtures, the field table and the paragraph after it. dt sets the fixture up in Go before a cell's first test and removes it after the last. A fixture mounts over NFS or SMB, not both. Settings: a fixture sets only settings the server has; pjdfstest and pynfs use squash: none, so root keeps its privileges; pynfs keeps lease: 30s until the server drops the setting. The lease: §4.2 'Settings' (the storage RFCs fix the NFSv4 lease at 90 s; pynfs keeps lease: 30s, so its lease-expiry tests each wait 30 s rather than 90). RFC 14 ('The lease period is fixed, not a setting', RFC 13) fixes the client lease at 90 s; RFC 29 §4.2 'Settings': fixtures use only settings the server has and change with it in the same pull request.
fixture.footer: A fixture sets only settings the server has. By design the client lease is fixed at 90 s, but today's server still lets it be set, so pynfs's test server uses 30 s and each lease-expiry test waits 30 s rather than 90. When the server drops the setting, the fixture drops it in the same change.

selfcheck.title: Before the first test, it checks itself
items: The DittoFS server answers.
When the cell uses Kerberos, the KDC answers before the server starts.
On a profile that stores data in S3, the bucket accepts a write and a read.
When the suite needs a mount, the share is mounted at the version asked for.
Every [[needs|need]] the suite declares is met.
selfcheck.rule: If a check fails, the [[cell]] ends with exit 2, which means [[not-run|not run]] and is never a pass. A failed fixture step is never retried either, because DittoFS itself starts inside the fixture and a retry could hide a flaky server.
selfcheck.footer: The fixture's own steps, such as installing packages, pulling images, building the server and starting it, share one timeout, 5 minutes by default. So a stalled package mirror fails the cell within minutes instead of using up its whole time limit.
selfcheck.notes: §4.2 (the self-check list; 'The silent passes in §1 are each a case of a missing check: the bucket, the NFS module, the Kerberos upcall'), §9 'Retrying a fixture's setup'. On 2026-10-07 (#2977) a stalled mirror used up 15 jobs' whole timeouts; the fixture's own 5-minute timeout (§4.2) ends such a stall early. The fixture's steps: §4.2 ('package installs, image pulls, building {bin}, the server's start').

bucket.title: The bucket refuses writes
bucket.notes: 'Start here · Scenarios', the second; §4.2 (self-check, never retried), §4.4 (exit 2). Outcome: a cell that tested nothing shows as not run instead of green. The RFC says the fixture checks the bucket; it doesn't say which process makes the probe write, so the arrow from dfs is the deck's simplification. Localstack is the S3 emulator the badger-s3 cells use, started as a service (§1's table, §4.5 service:localstack).

quizKdc.question: A [[cell]] uses Kerberos, and its KDC does not answer while the [[fixture]] starts. How does the cell end?
options: It passes, because its Kerberos tests skip and none of them fails.
The fixture's setup is retried until the KDC answers or time runs out.
It exits 2 before any test starts, which means not run and never a pass.
why: A skip read as a pass is how the old NFS `sec=krb5` job stayed green. Now the [[fixture]] checks the KDC before the server starts, so no test runs at all.
A failed [[fixture]] step is never retried, because DittoFS starts inside the fixture and a retry could hide a flaky server. Someone re-runs the cell by hand.
The [[fixture]]'s self-check fails before the first test, so nothing was tested. Exit 2 means [[not-run|not run]], and that is never counted as a pass.
quizKdc.notes: §4.2: the self-check list ('with kerberos, its KDC answers before the server starts'), 'a failed check ends the cell with exit 2, never a pass (R10)', and 'A failed fixture step is never retried (§9): DittoFS starts inside the fixture, so a retry could hide its flakiness … someone re-runs it by hand'. §4.4 exit 2. §1's table: the NFS sec=krb5 job exits 0 when the client can't load the NFS module.

places.title: Three places to run
table: its own system, or the [[dtc|dtc container]]
any suite whose needs the machine can meet
Linux with 4 CPUs, 16 GB of RAM and a 14 GB SSD, and also Windows and macOS
the `pr` and `merge` [[tier|tiers]], which run on each pull request and after each merge, and the nightly suites that fit
a large disk and room for long runs
the [[system-scenario|system scenarios]], long runs and the nightly performance comparison
places.footer: Each [[suite]] states its [[needs]], such as Linux, root, Docker or disk space. When the machine lacks one, `dt` can move the whole run into `dtc`, for example a Linux-only suite on macOS. If neither can meet it, the suite is [[not-run|not run]], with the reason. Without `--ci` it is just skipped. With `--ci`, the flag CI runs `dt` with, it is an error and exits 2.
places.notes: §4.5 Where a suite runs: the needs list, the places table, and 'For an unmet need, dt run either moves the whole run to the dtc container … or reports the suite as not run … It is never reported as passed.' In CI, dt plan gives each cell its place from its needs. --ci: §4.4's flags table ('non-interactive … a suite that can't run here is an error, not a skip'); §4.8, each run job is dt run CELL --tier T --ci. Moving to dtc: §4.4 --in auto, §4.5 ('macOS runs Linux-only suites in dtc').

dedicated.title: The [[dedicated-host|dedicated host]] is not a runner
items: GitHub's own guidance says self-hosted runners “should almost never be used for public repositories”.
So the dedicated host, `ditto`, runs `dt` from cron instead, and its nightly run tests only the latest commit on develop.
That nightly run takes only the cells GitHub's hosted runners cannot hold, such as the long [[system-scenario|system scenarios]] whose file names start with 9, one of which grows a 30 GB file.

Every 10 minutes it also checks develop, `main` and a long-lived feature branch. When one has a new commit and the host is idle, it runs the system scenarios on it and sets the commit status `system (dedicated)`.
Its GitHub token can write issues and commit statuses, and nothing else.
dedicated.notes: §4.5 'The dedicated host is not a self-hosted runner'; §9 'The dedicated host' (ditto, a server Cubbit rents; cloud spot VMs are the alternative). It runs only when nothing else runs on the host; merges landing during a run are taken together by the next one. Only develop's new failures go to the develop-status issue. The 9x scenarios: §4.5's places table (scenario 92 grows a 30 GB file) and §4.1's system entry (needs_by_test '9?-*.sh'). The branches the host watches are develop, main and feat/storage-v2 (§4.5). Scenario file names are <number>-<what>-<size>.sh; the long runs match 9?-*.sh (§4.1).

tiers.title: Four [[tier|tiers]]
table: every pull request, and the merge queue's run on the merged result
every push to develop, `main` or a long-lived feature branch
a nightly schedule, and the [[dedicated-host|dedicated host]]
`dt run NAME`, or a workflow started by hand
tiers.footer: Each tier runs everything the smaller one runs: `merge` includes `pr`, and `nightly` runs all but the `manual` suites. A [[suite]] names the smallest tier that runs it. Moving it is a one-word change, made on the timings `dt history` has measured.
tiers.notes: §4.3 Tiers (table and 'Budgets'); §9 'The tier budgets', adjusted on measured numbers. Before dt (October 2026) a PR waited 25–40 min. On 2026-10-12 a merge took a median of 33 minutes to its last check (§9). The pr tier also runs on merge_group: tests.yml maps that event to pr. The merge queue is enabled on develop and feat/storage-v2, so a queued pull request runs the pr tier again on the merged result (§4.3, §4.8). The merge tier runs on pushes to develop, main and feat/storage-v2 (§4.3).

whatruns.title: What each pull request runs
items: In every [[tier]], the conformance suites run only on `badger-s3`, the [[store-profile|store profile]] that production uses.
Tests are not chosen by which layer a change touched, because the components depend on each other too much for “only NFS changed” to be safe.
The exceptions are narrow suites that list `paths`. On a pull request they run only if it touches those paths, as e2e's Kerberos run does.
A pull request that changes only documentation plans no [[cell|cells]], so the [[gate]] waits only for the lint jobs.
smbtorture alone took 21–23 minutes on a pull request, so its tests are split into two [[test-shard|shards]] on two runners.
whatruns.notes: §4.3 'Conformance runs the production profile only', 'No selection by changed layer' (the second exception: cross-protocol e2e while the adapters move onto the VFS service, RFC 17 §9); §4.8 'Docs-only PRs'; §9 'The PR budget against smbtorture' (23 min on memory, 21 on badger). Note: §4.4 and §4.8 also let the unit cell on PRs test only the Go packages a change touched (--changed); the merge run tests them all. The gate needs plan, run and the three lint jobs, and the lint jobs don't wait for plan, so a docs-only change still has its commits and suite tables checked (§4.8 'Lint').

gate.title: One [[gate]] decides merges
jobs: The `plan` job runs `dt plan --tier T --json` to list the cells of tier T.
Each `run` job runs one [[cell]], with `dt run CELL --ci`.
The `gate` job waits for every [[blocking]] job, always runs, and fails unless each of them exited 0.
The `post` job reports failures, and it runs only on develop and on scheduled runs.
merge: The `gate` check passes, and so do the lint checks Go Checks, Repo Checks and ShellCheck, and the security scans gitleaks and CodeQL, whose check is named Analyze (go).
One reviewer has approved the pull request.
Before it lands, the pull request is tested again on top of the latest develop.
gate.notes: §4.8 CI, Jobs and Merging. Non-blocking cells run in a second matrix the gate doesn't wait for. The gate became required after the pr tier had been green for two weeks (§9), replacing Unit Tests and Integration Tests. A single gate that always runs avoids GitHub's path-filter trap. The last condition is the merge queue, which runs the pr tier on merge_group, on the merged result; the ruleset also still requires up-to-date branches (§4.8). Required checks: §4.8 'Merging' and 'Lint'; gitleaks and CodeQL (Analyze (go)) stay GitHub actions (§4.8, §5).

prrun.title: A pull request breaks one pjdfstest test
prrun.notes: 'Start here · Scenarios', the first; §4.3, §4.4 (exit 1), §4.7 (no retry on pull requests), §4.8 (gate). Outcome: the PR shows one red gate, and its report names the test. The test name chmod/12.t is from §4.6's illustrative summary.json.

quizPrFail.question: On a pull request, a pjdfstest test that no list names fails, though it might pass if run again. What happens?
options: Its cell exits 1 and the gate fails, because a PR never retries a test.
It runs once more, passes, and is graded flaky, so the gate passes.
Its cell exits 2, not run, because one failed attempt proves nothing.
why: No [[retry]] runs on a pull request, so the test is graded `new` and its [[cell]] exits 1. A [[blocking]] cell that did not exit 0 makes the [[gate]] fail.

In CI, a retry runs only on a push to develop, main or `feat/storage-v2`, which in practice follows a merge, and on scheduled runs. On a pull request nothing is retried, so a PR cannot merge a [[flaky]] test it introduced.
Exit 2 is for a test that did not run. This one ran and failed with no list entry, so it is a new failure and its [[cell]] exits 1.
quizPrFail.notes: 'Start here · Scenarios', the first: graded a new failure, exit 1 (§4.4); no retry on a pull request (§4.7 Retry: 'None on pull requests … so a PR can't merge a flaky test it introduced. On a push and on the schedule, --retry 1 …'); the gate fails because a blocking cell did not exit 0 (§4.8). Exit 2 means not run (§4.4). tests.yml runs on a push only to develop, main and feat/storage-v2, so a push is in practice a merge.

exit.title: Four exit statuses
table: no new failures, no unexpected skips, no unexpected passes
a new failure — a hang or a crash included — or an [[unexpected-pass|unexpected pass]]
a regression, or a list out of date
something did not run: a need was unmet under `--ci`, the [[fixture]] failed, no test ran, or, in a suite with a known-failure list, a test skipped without being listed
[[not-run|not run]]: something that should have been tested was not
the command was used wrongly, or the registry has an error
fix the command or the registry file
exit.footer: A [[cell]] that has both a new failure and something not run exits 1, and its report lists both. On develop, exit 1 raises the alert from its first run, while exit 2, an environment problem or lost coverage, alerts only after 2 runs in a row. That difference is the main defence against another flood of alerts.
exit.notes: §4.4, the exit status table and the paragraph after it; R10. Exit 2 also covers a fixture that timed out, tests a cell's timeout left unstarted, and a test whose output stopped before its result without a crash of the code under test. 'Green' (§2): no new failures, no unexpected skips and no unexpected passes. The alert: §4.8 'Develop goes red' (a run whose cells have new failures or unexpected passes after the retry posts; exit 2 alerts only after two consecutive runs of the cell) and §4.4 ('the main defence against another flood').

formats.title: Seven [[result-format|formats]], one reader each
table: lint, operator, `system` (the [[system-scenario|system scenarios]]), fio-verify, bench-smoke, cthon04
formats.footer: For every format except `exit`, the outcome comes from the tool's own results, not its exit status. Among the `exit` suites, `operator` tests the Kubernetes operator, `fio-verify` runs fio workloads on a mounted share, and `cthon04` and `nfstest` test what a kernel NFS client sees through a mount.
formats.notes: §4.6 Formats (abridged). dt adds -json -count=1 after go test, so no result is replayed from Go's cache. A crash of the code under test fails the test (exit 1); a client that died before the result leaves it incomplete (exit 2). A cell whose tool wrote no results is not run. The system suite runs the scenarios through setup.sh (§4.1). The suites: §4.1's registry (operator: make -C k8s/dittofs-operator test lint manifests-verify; fio-verify: dfsbench's workloads and the verify jobs, which read their data back; cthon04 and nfstest: what a kernel client sees through an untuned mount). Each reader keeps the rules of the grader its suite uses today (§4.6).

grades.title: Every result gets a [[grade]]
table: the test failed and no list entry matches it, or it crashed the code under test
the test failed and a [[known-failure|known-failure]] entry matches it
the test is on the [[quarantine]] list and no known-failure entry grades it first
the test is on a list, its entry is not marked `intermittent` (failing on some runs only), and it passed every time it ran in the cell
the test skipped and an [[expected-skip|expected-skip]] entry matches it
the test skipped, is not listed, and its suite keeps a known-failure file
the tool's output stopped before this test's result was written
grades.notes: §4.6 'Grades in CTRF and JUnit' (abridged). Also: a pass with no entry has no grade and passes; `ungraded` is a skip in a suite without a known file (a Go suite until it opts in), and passes. A Go parent test whose failing subtests are all known is known too. In CTRF a known failure is written as skipped with rawStatus failed, so a reader counts as failed only what makes the cell exit 1. intermittent: §4.7's known.yaml example ('it fails on some runs only; a pass is reported, not failed').

knownfile.title: A [[known-failure|known failure]] is data
items: Every entry says whether it will be fixed: `planned`, which names its issue, or `wontfix`. An entry without `fix` is an error.
Every entry has a reason and a category.
`where` limits an entry to some matrix values, [[tier|tiers]], options or operating systems.
A single matcher in `dt` reads every list. It accepts exact names, a name ending in `.*`, and shell globs.
knownfile.footer: One YAML file per [[suite]] replaces the old Markdown lists, and `dt known import` converts them once.
knownfile.notes: §4.7 'Known failures and expected skips' (the example entry is §4.7's own, its reason shortened here: 'NFSv4 silly rename: unlinking an open file renames it, so its link count stays 1'). Categories: bug, feature, env, proto, permanent. Today most rows name no issue (Appendix A).

skips.title: A skip must be [[expected-skip|expected]]
items: In a suite that keeps a known-failure file, a test that skips without being listed makes its [[cell]] exit 2.
The Go suites contain 331 `Skip` calls, so they adopt this rule one package at a time, starting with e2e. Until a package adopts it, its skips are counted but not graded.

With this rule, the 70 WPTS tests, the 11 SMB Kerberos subtests and 19 end-to-end error cases run across both NFS and SMB, which skipped as well, would each have shown as lost coverage the day they started skipping.
The first lists of expected skips are written from today's runs, each entry with a reason, so a new skip stands out.
skips.notes: §4.7 'Expected skips'; R10; §9 'Which Go suites grade their skips'. 71 test files also branch on testing.Short(). A run that names tests grades only those; a named test that skipped because of a test it depends on is not run (exit 2). The 19 cross-protocol error cases: §1's table, e2e row.

honest.title: A list must keep telling the truth
honest.pass: When a [[known-failure|known failure]] passes, the [[cell]] fails with exit 1, because the list no longer says what the server does. So a fix removes its own entry. If any test the entry matches still fails, the entry stays known. An entry marked `intermittent: true` reports such a pass instead of failing.
honest.msg: An entry may give a `message:`, text that the failure must contain. Say a test fails because the code it calls is a stub, a placeholder whose error starts with “stub:”. Listed with `message: "stub:"`, it turns red as soon as it fails for any other reason.
honest.notes: §4.7 'Unexpected pass' and 'Failing for the right reason'. An expected skip that runs and passes is an unexpected pass too; one that runs and fails is a new failure, unless a known-failure entry covers it. A flaky test with no entry belongs in quarantine, not under intermittent. The stub example: §4.7 'Failing for the right reason' ('so a known failure can't hide a second one'). What a stub is, is the deck's gloss.

flakes.title: [[flaky|Flaky]] tests: quarantine and retry
q: A quarantine entry names the suite, the test and an issue, and expires at most 90 days ahead.
The test still runs and its result is recorded, but its failure never fails a run or raises an alert.
A crash or a hang is still graded `new`, even in quarantine.
Once an entry has expired it excuses nothing, so its test fails as new. `dt doctor`, a check that every pull request runs, fails on the expired entry too.
r: Tests are never retried on a pull request, so a PR cannot merge a flaky test it introduced.
On a push to develop, main or `feat/storage-v2` (in practice, after a merge) and on scheduled runs, `--retry 1` runs each new failure once more, and nothing else.
A test that passes on retry is flaky. It raises no alert, and `dt history` counts it.
A test that is flaky twice in a week on develop becomes a candidate for quarantine.
flakes.notes: §4.7 'Quarantine' and 'Retry'. The quarantine list is test/harness/quarantine.yaml; an entry names one test exactly, never a pattern. An expired entry is an error from dt doctor, which lint-repo runs (Repo Checks). The retry runs on the cell's own fixture, within the cell's limit; a test none of the naming rules can name isn't retried. The AD-DC keytab race (#2968) is what quarantine is for. Expiry: §4.7 ('its test fails as new and the gate goes red on that test and on Repo Checks'); dt doctor is one of lint-repo's commands (§4.1), and lint-repo is the Repo Checks job, which runs on every pull request (§4.8). tests.yml runs on a push only to develop, main and feat/storage-v2, so a push is in practice a merge.

ctrf.title: One result format: [[ctrf|CTRF]], with JUnit beside it
items: JUnit XML has no formal specification and no field for a retry or a flaky pass — but CI services read it, and none reads CTRF natively yet.
CTRF is a JSON schema with fields for retries, flaky passes and the tool's own status. `dt` pins version 0.1.0 and stores its [[grade]] in the `extra` field.
JUnit files are generated from the CTRF results, for Codecov and other tools that read JUnit.
`summary.json` is rewritten after every [[cell]], so a stopped run still reports what finished.
ctrf.notes: §4.6 (results directory, the CTRF example, 'Why CTRF, with JUnit beside it', 'In CI'). The example's numbers are illustrative, as the RFC says. Each cell's server log is kept as dfs.log in its results directory.

quizFixed.question: A PR fixes the bug behind a [[known-failure|known failure]] but keeps its entry, not marked `intermittent`. What happens?
options: The cell stays green, since a test that passes can never fail its cell.
The cell exits 1, because the list no longer says what the server does.
The cell exits 2, because a result that contradicts its list is not run.
why: A pass is graded against the lists too. A [[known-failure|known failure]] that passes is an [[unexpected-pass|unexpected pass]], and that makes the [[cell]] exit 1.
Kept, the entry would hide the test's next regression. So the [[unexpected-pass|unexpected pass]] fails the [[cell]], and the fix must remove its own entry.
Exit 2 means something was not tested, but this test ran. An [[unexpected-pass|unexpected pass]] counts with the new failures, so the [[cell]] exits 1.
quizFixed.notes: §4.7 'Unexpected pass': 'A known failure that passes … fails the cell (exit 1): its entry no longer says what the server does, and a list that keeps it would hide the test's next regression. A fix PR removes its own entry, and its run fails until it does.' intermittent: true reports the pass instead. §4.4: exit 1 includes an unexpected pass; exit 2 is not run.

redrun.title: After a merge: flaky, then really broken
redrun.notes: 'Start here · Scenarios', the third and fourth; §4.4 'Posting failures'; §4.7 Retry; §4.8 'Develop goes red'. The posting is done by tests.yml's post job, from develop and nightly runs only. The test names are from §4.6's illustrative summary.json. Guardrails on per-test issues (§4.4): posted only from develop and nightly runs, never from pull requests or laptops; one issue per cell and test, found again by the develop-red label and the title 'CELL TEST fails on develop'; dt never closes a test's issue; only results graded new get one; more than 10 new failures post no per-test issues; an issue carries the test, its failing line, the commit and the log link, nothing about customers or deployments.

flood.title: Why it shouldn't flood this time
table: one status issue, rewritten in place, plus per-test issues after 2 failing runs in a row
only when the failing set changes
can be quarantined, and then never counts
alerts after 2 runs in a row
flood.footer: [[known-failure|Known failures]], expected skips and quarantined tests never raise an alert. E-mail comes from GitHub's own notifications for the issue, so the repository holds no mail secrets.
flood.notes: §4.8 'Develop goes red', including 'The removed alarm already retried once and kept a single issue. It still flooded, because it sent mail on every red run and couldn't tell a flaky subtest from a regression (#1705).' R7.

bench.title: Performance is tracked, not gated
items: GitHub's hosted runners share hardware, so their timings are too noisy to fail a pull request over a percentage drop.
`bench-smoke` checks that the benchmarks still work. It does not block pull requests, but it does block the runs after a merge and at night.

The throughput and allocation checks, also called gates, fail when a measurement crosses a threshold. They skip under Go's race detector (`-race`) and short mode (`-short`), which the `unit` suite uses, so no job ran them.
`unit --nonrace` runs them every night without those flags. One that still trips after its retry turns the nightly run red, but it never fails a pull request.
bench.notes: §4.10 Benchmarks and long runs; §4.6 Metrics. A tripped nonrace gate on the retry turns the nightly run red and posts, and fails no PR. The gates skipping under -race and -short, with no job running them: §1's table, last row. The unit suite runs go test -race, with -short on pull requests; its nonrace option runs the two gate tests nightly (§4.1).

baseline.title: Each benchmark against its own baseline
items: After every merge, the benchmarks of each component that names one run again, and `benchstat` compares them with that component's stored baseline.
A change beyond `benchstat`'s noise band is posted for people to look at; it never fails the run. A baseline is replaced only through a pull request.

`perf-night` on the [[dedicated-host|dedicated host]] runs the same SMB workload against DittoFS and against Samba, which serves only as a reference point for the test. It flags a night whose figures fall below their own recent median, but the flag fails nothing. The figures hold for that one machine, say nothing about either server in general, and are not meant to be reproduced elsewhere. `dt history` records them, and they never decide whether a run passes.
baseline.notes: §4.10 Benchmarks and long runs, 'Comparison against a stored baseline'; §4.6 Metrics. After every merge, a step also runs the benchmarks of the components that name one and compares them with their stored baseline using benchstat. A change beyond benchstat's noise band is posted, never a failed run, and a baseline is replaced only through a pull request (§4.10, 'Comparison against a stored baseline'). perf-night flags a point, an area or the night's figure below its 7-day median by more than its noise band; the cell fails when a step fails or times out, or the night can't be scored.

whom.dev: One command, `dt run NAME`, the same as CI's. `dt doctor` says what the machine lacks and how to get it. `dt` runs as you, and calls `sudo -n` only for steps that need root.
whom.rev: The [[gate]] is the one test check they wait for, beside the lint and security checks. A red PR names the failing test, and a red develop shows up as one issue rather than a storm of e-mails.
whom.auth: They write no setup script: a need becomes a new [[fixture]] field, with a test. Every expected failure and skip is listed with a reason, and a bug also gets an issue.
whom.notes: This slide is the deck's framing, from §3 ('Getting dt', sudo), §4.4 (dt doctor), §4.8, §4.2 and §4.7.

rules.title: What the harness must do
items: There is one entry point, and it runs the same way on a laptop and in CI.
Adding a suite takes one line. Services, the matrix, fixtures, grading and reports need no code written for that suite.
The tests and the rules of today's graders are kept, and each suite's scripts are replaced by a fixture. The scripts are deleted once `dt` gives the same results for that suite.
A result that is [[not-run|not run]] is never reported as a pass.
Every RFC names, in a paragraph of its own, the suites that test its component, and `dt docs --check` checks those names against the registry.
rules.footer: “Green” means no new failures, no unexpected skips and no unexpected passes.
rules.notes: §2 Requirements: R1, R3 and R5, R9, R10, R11 (abridged), and the definition of green under the table. Also R2 (a specified YAML registry), R4 (runs tracked by the harness), R6 (tiers, no selection by changed layer), R7 (an alert without a flood), R8 (external-tool suites first, and green). R9 ('keep what's tested, replace what isn't'; the graders' rules carry over, each suite's scripts give way to a fixture once its results match). R11 (every RFC under docs/internals/rfcs/ has a paragraph naming its suites, §4.9).

doubles.title: Test doubles: three kinds, and no stubs
doubles.lead: A test runs against the real code that the code under test talks to. A stand-in for that code, called a test double, is allowed in three kinds only.
ok: An injected clock or a seeded random source, because time and chance are inputs to the code.
An in-memory version that passes the same conformance tests as the real one. The in-memory block store passes the same tests as the S3 store.
A wrapper around a real part that fails, delays or crashes on cue, such as a store that fails its third write.
bad: A canned stub written for one test, like a fake S3 client that always returns one error.
A fake that counts calls so that a test can check which calls were made.
Any double that no conformance tests hold to the real code.
Swapping a package-level variable to change what the code does.
doubles.footer: An error a test needs comes from a fault wrapper, never from a stub. External systems, such as S3 or a Kerberos KDC, are tested for real in the integration suite.
doubles.notes: §4.11 Test doubles. The three kinds: inputs (an injected clock, a seeded random source); a verified in-memory implementation that lives with the package owning the interface and passes the same conformance suite as the production one; fault injection, a wrapper around a real implementation or a kind 2 that fails, delays, tears or crashes on cue ('An error answer a test needs is given this way, by a fault wrapper, not by a stub'). Also allowed: a wrapper that records each call and passes it through, when the call reaching a dependency is itself the requirement. Not doubles at all: a sink that keeps what the code delivered, a per-OS table (data), a tunable passed through the constructor, a Null service used as a load, a hook set per instance from export_test.go. Banned: 'a canned stub written for one test; a recording or counting fake used to check which calls were made; a double that no conformance suite holds to the real one; swapping a package-level variable'. External systems (a KDC, a domain controller, an LDAP directory, S3) are tested for real in integration; a stand-in runs in unit only as a kind 2 whose conformance suite also runs against the real system. Every RFC's test strategy is bound by it, and CLAUDE.md's 'Writing tests' repeats it for every contributor. The examples are the deck's own: the in-memory block store is pkg/block/remote/memory, held with the S3 store to blockstoretest.RemoteBlockStoreConformance; the fake S3 client and the third-write fault are illustrations.

nochange.title: What this doesn't change
keep: The tests themselves, and the known failures they are graded against
The names of the required checks: Go Checks, Repo Checks, ShellCheck
out: `combined-tree`, which merges open PRs to test them together
The canary, which watches a live deployment
The job that runs nfstest against the kernel's own NFS server, knfsd, used only as a reference for the test results
nochange.notes: §5 What this doesn't change; §4.8 'Four things stay outside the registry'; §4.1 'What isn't registered' (the NFS sec=krb5 job, covered by e2e; the crash rigs and edge tests, runnable by hand). The tests' skips are now graded, which is new.

risks.title: Risks, and what answers them
table: One bug in `dt` breaks all of CI
`dt`'s own tests run on every PR, and each old job keeps running until `dt`'s cells give the same results, unless it ran the same commands as `dt`
the `merge` tier runs after every merge, so a miss costs one red develop instead of a regression nobody sees
every entry has a reason, bug entries name an issue, an unexpected pass fails the run, and `dt known prune` removes entries no recent run needed
entries expire and need an issue, and quarantined results are still recorded
A fixture misses what a script did
the old job runs beside `dt` until their per-test results match on 5 consecutive runs
risks.notes: §7 Risks (abridged). Also: posted issues flooding or leaking (§4.4's guardrails) and CTRF changing under us (one pinned version, JUnit beside it).

steps: Before `dt`, a CI job ran `run.sh`, which ran the suite's own scripts, and only those scripts ran the test tool.
The code that set up the DittoFS server was copied from script to script, in at least five places, and those copies are where the passes that tested nothing came from.
With RFC 29, CI runs `dt`, which builds the server itself as a [[fixture]] and calls the test tool directly, with no script in between.
The pull request runs the `pr` [[tier]], where pjdfstest runs only on `badger-s3`, the [[store-profile|store profile]] production uses.
One test fails, and no [[known-failure|known-failure]] list contains it. So it is [[grade|graded]] `new`, and its [[cell]] exits 1.
No [[retry]] runs on a pull request, so a [[flaky]] test can't sneak in.
The [[gate]] fails, because a [[blocking]] cell did not exit 0. The report of the run names the failing test.
Before the first test runs, the [[fixture]] checks itself. First it finds that the server answers.
Next, the S3 bucket must accept a write and a read. In tests, localstack, a local stand-in for S3, serves the bucket of the `badger-s3` profile. It refuses the write, so the check fails.
Because the check failed, no test runs. The [[cell]] exits with status 2, which means [[not-run|not run]] and is never counted as a pass.
A failed fixture step is never retried automatically, so someone has to re-run the cell by hand.
After a merge, the `merge` [[tier]] runs, and one test fails.
`--retry 1` runs only that test again, and this time it passes, so it is graded [[flaky]]. No issue opens, and `dt history` counts the flaky pass.
After another merge, a test still fails after its [[retry]], so the run exits 1. The single [[develop-red|develop-red issue]] opens, or is updated if it is already open.
If the test fails 2 runs in a row, it also gets an issue of its own, unless more than 10 tests are failing at once.
The develop-red issue closes once every test in its list passes again in the tier that runs it, or has been listed as known or quarantined.
